items.followUp: Name any two metals that are highly reactive.

rubric.why: One mark for naming a very reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award this mark for any one correct example from the model answer or another very reactive metal.

rubric.why: A second correct example is required for the second mark.
rubric.description: Names a second very reactive metal.
rubric.how: Award this mark for another correct example; do not award it for repeating the same metal.

modelAnswer: Sodium and potassium are two very reactive metals.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of magnesium oxide by ionic bonding.

rubric.why: The formation of the sodium ion begins with loss of an electron.
rubric.description: States that a sodium atom loses one electron.
rubric.how: Award for correctly describing electron loss by sodium.

rubric.why: The chlorine atom accepts the electron lost by sodium.
rubric.description: States that a chlorine atom gains one electron.
rubric.how: Award for correctly describing electron gain by chlorine.

rubric.why: Electron transfer forms oppositely charged ions.
rubric.description: Identifies the sodium and chloride ions formed.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the positive sodium ion and negative chloride ion.

rubric.why: The ionic bond is the attraction between the oppositely charged ions in sodium chloride.
rubric.description: Explains that attraction between the ions forms the ionic bond in NaCl.
rubric.how: Award for naming the electrostatic attraction as the ionic bond, in the context of NaCl.

modelAnswer: A sodium atom has one electron in its outer shell, while a chlorine atom needs one electron to complete its outer shell.
Sodium transfers its outer electron to chlorine.
Sodium forms a positive Na⁺ ion and chlorine forms a negative Cl⁻ ion.
The electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions forms the ionic bond in sodium chloride (NaCl).

items.followUp: Differentiate between a monoatomic molecule and a polyatomic molecule, giving an example of each.

rubric.why: A homoatomic molecule consists of atoms of the same element.
rubric.how: Award for stating that its atoms are of the same kind or element.

rubric.why: An example supports the definition but is not needed for the two-mark distinction.
rubric.description: Provides an example of a homoatomic molecule.
rubric.how: Do not allocate a separate mark; use as evidence alongside the definition if required.

rubric.why: A heteroatomic molecule contains atoms of different elements.
rubric.how: Award for stating that its atoms are of different kinds or elements.

modelAnswer: A homoatomic molecule consists of atoms of the same element, for example O₂.
A heteroatomic molecule consists of atoms of different elements, for example H₂O.

items.followUp: Write the empirical formula of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, and explain how it is obtained.

rubric.why: The empirical formula expresses the simplest ratio of atoms in a compound.
rubric.description: Defines empirical formula as the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms.
rubric.how: Award for describing the simplest whole-number ratio of the constituent atoms.

rubric.why: Glucose has the empirical formula CH₂O.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of an empirical formula.
rubric.how: Award for giving CH₂O as the empirical formula of glucose, or another correct empirical-formula example.

modelAnswer: An empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound.
For example, the empirical formula of glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is CH₂O.

items.followUp: Write any two properties of a proton.

rubric.why: A neutron has no electric charge.
rubric.description: States that a neutron is electrically neutral.
rubric.how: Award for identifying its zero charge.

rubric.why: A neutron has a mass of approximately one atomic mass unit.
rubric.how: Award for approximately 1 u or 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg; another correct property, such as its location in the nucleus, may also earn the mark.

modelAnswer: A neutron has no electric charge; it is electrically neutral.
Its mass is approximately 1 atomic mass unit (about 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
Neutrons are present in the nucleus of an atom.

items.followUp: Why do isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but different atomic masses?

rubric.why: Atomic number is the number of protons and determines an element's identity.
rubric.description: Links atomic number to proton number and elemental identity.
rubric.how: Award for stating that proton number determines which element an atom is.

rubric.why: Atomic number determines electron arrangement and chemical properties, whereas atomic mass can differ between isotopes.
rubric.description: Contrasts atomic number with the variation in atomic mass among isotopes.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that isotopes have the same proton number but different neutron numbers/masses, or that atomic number determines chemical properties.

modelAnswer: Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom and determines the identity of the element and its electronic configuration.
Atomic mass can vary between isotopes of the same element because they have different numbers of neutrons.

items.followUp: Why is the first ionization energy of potassium less than that of calcium?

rubric.why: Magnesium has a greater nuclear charge than sodium in the same period.
rubric.description: Compares the nuclear charges of sodium and magnesium.
rubric.how: Award for stating that magnesium has more protons or a greater nuclear charge.

accept: holds its outer electron more strongly
rubric.why: Magnesium attracts its outer electron more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove it than from sodium.
rubric.description: Explains why sodium has the lower ionization energy.
rubric.how: Award for linking the stronger attraction in magnesium to the greater energy needed to remove its electron.

modelAnswer: Sodium and magnesium are in the same period, but magnesium has a greater nuclear charge.
Magnesium attracts its outer electron more strongly, so more energy is needed to remove it; therefore, sodium has the lower ionization energy.

items.followUp: Define electronegativity and state one factor that affects it.

rubric.why: Electron affinity is associated with energy released when an atom accepts an electron.
rubric.description: States the energy change involved in electron affinity.
rubric.how: Award for stating that energy is released when the electron is added.

rubric.why: The definition refers to an electron being added to a neutral gaseous atom.
rubric.description: Identifies the atom that accepts the electron and gives the unit.
rubric.how: Award for specifying a neutral gaseous atom and a correct unit: kJ mol⁻¹ or eV per atom.

modelAnswer: Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to a neutral gaseous atom to form a negative ion.
Its unit is kJ mol⁻¹ (or eV per atom).
